question: A patient presents with well-defined, milky-white patches on the dorsa of the hands. What distinguishes these vitiligo lesions from the pale patches of a hypopigmenting condition such as pityriasis alba?

answers.text: Vitiligo patches are completely depigmented (milky-white) with sharp borders because melanocytes are destroyed, whereas pityriasis alba patches are only hypopigmented (dull, off-white) with ill-defined borders because melanocytes survive but produce less melanin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In vitiligo, autoimmune destruction of melanocytes causes complete depigmentation — milky- or chalk-white, sharply bordered patches. In pityriasis alba and other hypopigmenting conditions, melanocytes survive but are underactive, yielding dull, ill-defined, partially pale patches.

answers.text: Vitiligo patches are slightly paler than surrounding skin, while pityriasis alba patches are chalk-white

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This reverses the relationship. Vitiligo produces complete depigmentation (milky-white), while pityriasis alba produces only partial hypopigmentation (slightly paler, ill-defined).

answers.text: Vitiligo is distinguished by fine powdery scale on the surface of the patches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fine powdery scale is a feature of pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor), not vitiligo. Vitiligo patches have no surface change and no scaling.

answers.text: No clinically visible difference exists; a biopsy is always required to distinguish them

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The distinction between depigmentation and hypopigmentation is a clinical one visible to the trained eye and enhanced by a Wood's lamp, which makes vitiligo patches glow bright chalky blue-white.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is the degree and quality of colour change: vitiligo = milky-white, sharp borders, complete depigmentation (melanocytes destroyed); hypopigmentation = dull, ill-defined, partial paleness (melanocytes present but underactive). The Wood's lamp accentuates vitiligo as bright blue-white.
Correct. The milky-white, sharply bordered depigmentation of vitiligo — reflecting complete melanocyte loss — is the first and most useful bedside discriminator from hypopigmenting conditions.
